title: Wien Bridge Oscillator: 5 Expert Steps for Clean Sine Waves
text:
Analog Electronics

 Wien Bridge Oscillator: 5 Expert Steps for Clean Sine Waves

 Two resistors, two capacitors and one op amp can produce a sine wave pure enough for audio testing. The secret is holding the amplifier gain at exactly three, and the way you do that decides how clean the output really is.

 
 f = 1/(2πRC) 
 Gain of 3 
 Lamp Stabilisation 
 Diode and JFET AGC 
 Low Distortion 
 




 The Wien bridge oscillator is the classic low distortion sine wave source for audio and test work. This guide covers its frequency formula, the gain of three condition, amplitude stabilisation methods and a full design example.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a Wien bridge oscillator works, why it needs a gain of exactly three, how lamps, diodes and JFETs stabilise its amplitude and how to design one step by step.


 
 
 
 What Is a Wien Bridge Oscillator?


 A Wien bridge oscillator is a sine wave oscillator that uses a series RC and a parallel RC network as frequency selective positive feedback around a non inverting amplifier. At one frequency the network has zero phase shift and passes one third of the output back, so an amplifier gain of three keeps the oscillation going.


 It is usually built with an operational amplifier , and it works best from a few hertz to a few hundred kilohertz. Students meet it alongside the other types of transistor oscillators , but it stands out for its low distortion and easy tuning.


 
 
 Image credit: Learn About Electronics . Image courtesy of Learn About Electronics, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Learn About Electronics built a test circuit with 10 kΩ resistors and 100 nF capacitors. The calculated frequency was 159 Hz and the measured frequency was 157 Hz, which shows how closely the simple formula predicts a real circuit.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 How the RC Bridge Selects One Frequency


 The feedback path has a series R and C going to the non inverting input and a parallel R and C from that input to ground. At low frequency the series capacitor blocks the signal, and at high frequency the parallel capacitor shorts it, much like the two halves of an RC low pass and high pass filter placed back to back.


 Exactly at the centre frequency the output of this band pass network is in phase with its input and equal to one third of it. Any other frequency gets both a phase error, explained in phase angle in AC circuits , and extra attenuation, so the loop cannot sustain it.


 
 Power On Noise contains all frequencies

 RC Network Filters Only f0 returns in phase

 Gain Above 3 Amplitude grows at f0

 Stabiliser Acts Gain falls toward 3

 Steady Sine Constant amplitude output




 The second half of the bridge is the negative feedback divider RF and RG that sets the amplifier gain. Together the two arms form a bridge similar to the Wheatstone bridge , which is where the circuit gets its name.


 Do You Know?
 Max Wien described his bridge in 1891 for measuring impedance, long before it became an oscillator. William Hewlett used it with a small lamp for amplitude control in the HP 200A audio oscillator, the first product of Hewlett Packard.



 Wien Bridge Oscillator Frequency Formula


 When both resistors are equal to R and both capacitors are equal to C, the frequency and gain conditions become very simple. Texas Instruments engineers Ron Mancini and Richard Palmer state the requirement as an amplifier gain A of 3, with RF equal to twice RG.


 
 f0 = 1 ÷ (2π × R × C) 
 Gain = 1 + RF ÷ RG = 3, so RF = 2 × RG 

Example:
R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF, RG = 10 kΩ
R × C = 10000 × 0.00000001 = 0.0001 s
f0 = 1 ÷ (6.2832 × 0.0001) = 1591.5 Hz
 f0 = 1.59 kHz, RF = 20 kΩ 



 The TI application report used similar values and calculated 1.59 kHz, while the built circuit oscillated at 1.57 kHz. Component tolerance and op amp phase shift explain the small difference, so always trim the final frequency on the bench.

 Enter R in kilohms and C in nanofarads, since kΩ times nF gives microseconds. In practice RF is made slightly larger than twice RG so that oscillation starts reliably, and a stabiliser then pulls the gain back to three.

 Why the Gain Must Be Exactly Three


 If the loop gain is even slightly below one, the oscillation dies away. If it is slightly above one, the amplitude keeps growing until the op amp output hits the supply rails, which flattens the peaks and adds harmonics, the problem described in harmonic distortion and THD .


 The TI report shows that a plain circuit without any gain control had about 2.8 percent distortion, mainly from clipping at the rails. Fixed resistors alone can never hold the gain at exactly three, because they drift with temperature and age.


 The answer is a nonlinear or automatic gain control element that lowers the gain as the amplitude rises. This is the same loop gain idea studied with a Bode plot and gain margin , except that here we want the loop to sit right at the edge.


 Quick Tip
 Use film or C0G ceramic capacitors and 1 percent metal film resistors in the bridge. Ordinary high K ceramic capacitors change value with voltage and add distortion of their own.



 Amplitude Stabilisation Methods Compared


 
 Incandescent Lamp
 A small lamp replaces RG, and its resistance rises as it warms, cutting the gain.
 Best for: lowest distortion audio sources
 Classic 

 NTC Thermistor
 A thermistor replaces RF, and its resistance falls as it heats.
 Best for: compact low frequency designs
 Thermal 

 Diode Limiter
 Back to back diodes across part of RF reduce gain on the peaks.
 Best for: simple, low cost circuits
 Simple
